claim: PostgreSQL project, nbtree README: against a classic B-tree, the design it follows (L&Y) adds a right-link pointer to each page, to the page's right sibling.
PostgreSQL project, nbtree README: a split flags the left page INCOMPLETE_SPLIT until the parent has its downlink.
PostgreSQL project, nbtree README: before 9.4 incomplete splits were finished immediately at the end of recovery; now they are finished lazily at the next insertion or vacuum.
PostgreSQL project, nbtree README: a page is removed only when completely empty of items; merging partly-full pages is called impractical.
PostgreSQL project, nbtree README: the rightmost page of a level is never deleted, so the height of the tree cannot decrease.
MySQL 8.0 reference manual (self-reported): InnoDB tries to leave 1/16 of a page free for future insertions and updates.
MySQL 8.0 reference manual (self-reported): index records inserted in sequential order leave pages about 15/16 full, and records inserted in random order leave pages from 1/2 to 15/16 full.
MySQL 8.0 reference manual (self-reported): when an index page's fill factor drops below MERGE_THRESHOLD, which is 50% by default, InnoDB tries to contract the index tree to free the page.
Dong et al 2017 (RocksDB, CIDR 2017; self-reported): B-tree pages are only 1/2 to 2/3 full, as measured in Facebook production databases.

Dong et al 2017 (RocksDB, CIDR 2017; self-reported): storage used by RocksDB is about 50% lower than the space used by InnoDB with compression (baseline InnoDB with compression; workloads LinkBench, TPC-C and a review of Facebook MySQL installations).
note: The workloads in the claim are the collect file's list; TPC-C is named at paper.txt:34 and 101, not on the cited lines 341-352.

claim: Dong et al 2017 (RocksDB, CIDR 2017; self-reported): the data RocksDB writes to storage is between 10% and 15% of what InnoDB writes out (baseline InnoDB).
Dong et al 2017 (RocksDB, CIDR 2017; self-reported): the number and volume of reads is 10% - 20% higher in RocksDB than for InnoDB.
Dong et al 2017 (RocksDB, CIDR 2017; self-reported): in LinkBench the write volume per transaction is less than 20% of the volume of data written by InnoDB.
Matsunobu et al 2020 (MyRocks; self-reported): MyRocks reduced the instance size by 62.3% compared to compressed InnoDB.
Matsunobu et al 2020 (MyRocks; self-reported): approximately 25% to 30% of each InnoDB block space was wasted.

Matsunobu et al 2020 (MyRocks; self-reported): B-tree defragmentation was less effective than expected, because a continuous stream of mostly random writes quickly fragmented pages that had just been defragmented.
Matsunobu et al 2020 (MyRocks): the bulk load could load indexes directly into the LSM-tree, bypassing all MemTable writes and compactions.
Dong et al 2021 (RocksDB, FAST 2021; self-reported): running LinkBench on MySQL, RocksDB issues only 5% as many writes per transaction as InnoDB, a B-tree based storage engine.
Dong et al 2021 (RocksDB, FAST 2021; self-reported): leveled compaction write amplification in the 10-30 range is too high for write-heavy applications.
Dong et al 2021 (RocksDB, FAST 2021; self-reported): Tiered Compaction brings write amplification down to the 4-10 range, although with lower read performance.
Dong et al 2021 (RocksDB, FAST 2021; self-reported): of 42 production deployments, most of the workloads are space constrained.
Dong et al 2021 (RocksDB, FAST 2021), lesson 2: space efficiency is the bottleneck for most applications using SSDs.

Zhou et al 2021 (FoundationDB, SIGMOD 2021): the storage engine is an unversioned SQLite B-tree plus in-memory multi-versioned redo log data, and only mutations leaving the MVCC window are written to SQLite.
Zhou et al 2021 (FoundationDB, SIGMOD 2021; self-reported): FoundationDB chooses a 5-second MVCC window to limit the memory usage of the transaction system and storage servers.
Zhou et al 2021 (FoundationDB, SIGMOD 2021): many transactions that exceed the time limit 'can be divided into smaller transactions'.

Discord engineering blog 2023 (self-reported; the store and the service in front changed together, so not a controlled comparison): the move went from 177 Cassandra nodes to 72 ScyllaDB nodes, and each ScyllaDB node has 9 TB of disk space, up from the average of 4 TB per Cassandra node.

Discord engineering blog 2023 (self-reported; not a controlled comparison): fetching historical messages had a p99 of 40-125ms on Cassandra against 15ms on ScyllaDB, and inserts went from 5-70ms p99 on Cassandra to a steady 5ms p99.
Discord engineering blog 2023 (self-reported): after the migrator checkpointed token ranges locally, the migration's estimated time to completion was cut from three months to nine days.
Discord engineering blog 2023: request coalescing means that if several users request the same row at the same time, the database is queried once.
Discord engineering blog 2023 (self-reported): when a hot partition was encountered, it frequently affected latency across the entire database cluster.
Uber engineering blog 2016 (self-reported; Internet Archive copy): when a tuple location changes in Postgres, all indexes must be updated.
Uber engineering blog 2016 (self-reported; worked example, no baseline): a one-row update in Postgres writes the new tuple and adds a record to each of three indexes.
Uber engineering blog 2016 (self-reported): because replication happens at the physical level, we could end up completely corrupting our database indexes.
Uber engineering blog 2016 (self-reported): the repair, resyncing the replicas from a new snapshot, was 'a laborious process'.
WiredTiger architecture guide (B-tree): pages split once their configured limit is reached, causing the B-tree to expand.
WiredTiger architecture guide (B-tree): updates are 'chained into an update list' on the leaf page, so an entry may hold old or deleted values.
CockroachDB Pebble design note: compaction pacing uses an estimate of compaction debt and aims to 'keep the compaction debt at a constant level'.
Chu and others (LMDB source, lmdb.h): only one write transaction may be active at a time, which guarantees that writers can never deadlock, while readers run with no locks.
Chu and others (LMDB source, lmdb.h): read transactions prevent reuse of pages freed by newer write transactions, so the database can grow quickly.
Chu and others (LMDB source, mdb.c): on an append the new key starts the new page (split_indx = newindx; nkeys = 0); otherwise the split is at the middle, split_indx = (nkeys+1) / 2.
Chu and others (LMDB source, mdb.c; self-reported): the minimum page fill factor is 250 in tenths of a percent, and pages emptier than this are candidates for merging.
